Hi all,

I have a question about multiple covariate distance sampling (MCDS) and I can’t find an answer for it anywhere on here or on the online material – apologies I’ve missed it. The AIC score for my MCDS model with 'habitat' as a covariate (2 levels: scrubland:27; woodland: 142) is much lower than the models without this covariate and after inspecting the graphs I have chosen it as my best model. I don't have enough data for each of the levels to stratify by each level (should be 60-80 detections per level; Buckland et al. 2015 page 23) but was wondering if it is possible to obtain density estimates for each of the habitat types through MCDS? Can I use the scale coefficients (in bold) to calculate this? On page 90 of Buckland et al. (2015) table 5.9 appears to have density estimates for each tree type, but I'm not sure how to obtain them for my data in R.

trunk <- 100

dist.bins <- seq(0, trunk, length.out = 10)

kcovmod <- ds(ken, key = "hn", formula = ~ Habitat,

                 convert.units = 0.001, dht.group = FALSE, truncation = trunk, cutpoints = dist.bins)

Grace

Judging from your output, you did not design your survey such that you had strata that were the two habitat types, with transects fully within a stratum.  Instead, your transects crossed habitat boundaries, with part of a transect in "brushland" and the remainder in "woodland".  Do I have that correct?

If I have guessed correctly, then you can use the answer I provided to the list 10 days ago (22Aug19) treating species as a covariate.  This would require installing updates to R packages on which we are currently working.

This is an instance of post-stratification, where the stratification criterion (habitat in your situation) was not explicit in the survey design.

Have a look at the package updating process and syntax for using the function dht2 in this email thread on the list  https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/distance-sampling/vYc5CzfM86Y  Substitute the word "species" in that email exchange with "habitat" for your situation.  Let us know if that accomplishes what you wish.  Recognise also that elements of the new packages are relatively untested.

Grace

I see 9 detections not given either of the two habitat classifications; do you eliminate them from the analysis?

You have the habitat-specific abundance estimates; to convert abundance to density: divide abundance by area (200.1284 in your summary).  The CV for density is the same as the CV for abundance (you're dividing by a known constant).

But life would be easier if you assigned the output of dht2 to an object, then used print() on that object, with a report argument:

print(my.dht2.output, report="density")

We are working to estimate the spatial abundance of sheep in a ranch using DSM approach. We have a scale of segment and grid of 500m side, and a total of 74 segments. We calculate abundance with the classic distance sampling approach (based on design) and that gives us about 3000 animals, quite close to the real value, which we believe suggests that the problem is not our sampling design.

What do you think is happening?
Any advice will be very helpfull!

Thanks in advance
Natalia

Hi Irene, hi listfolk,

Not sure if you mean choosing cutpoints to use to analyse the data as
grouped distances or just for displaying the fitted detection function?

In both cases it's worth bearing in mind that you care more about what
the detection function is doing close to 0 distance (this also has a
larger effect on what your estimate of detection probability is).

shoulder of the function) and fewer, larger bins at larger distances
lets you see how well the function is fitting the data where it matters.

For fitting group distances there is quite a lot of information from p
259 onwards in the 2001 Introduction to Distance Sampling book by
Buckland et al.

Hope that helps!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicolás,

Just a wee warning - if your main interest is in looking at the effect of various environmental factors on relative abundance of different species, and you have used a global detection function over all species, you might need to keep an eye on whether any of your environmental factors (e.g. along the lines of habitat type, tree density, ground vegetation height etc.) might have species-specific effects on detectability. For example, tall grass might not affect detectability of giraffe, but probably would affect that of a small animal like duiker. If this is the case, you might be better off opting for several detection functions, with species you would expect to share similar patterns in detectability (i.e. in response to the relevant environmental variation) grouped together. You might also need to have one or more environmental variables included in your detection function.

I think this is more or less what you are suggesting in your last question. Anyway, with regard to exactly how to specify the relevant models, and including 'deflection effects', others on this forum will likely be much better able to advise than I can. But your instinct that detection functions including both giraffe and duiker registrations may cause problems is probably a good one!

Cheers,

Mark

Bearing in mind Mark Wilson's advice earlier in the thread, from a
coding perspective, dsm makes this simple. All you need to do is subset
your observation data.frame correctly and dsm() will pick out the
correct data.

So, say you have your observation frame, called obsdata and it has a
column called "species" which has which species your observation is
from. Let's say you are interested in the species "babelfish", you can

obsdata_babel <- subset(obsdata, species=="babelfish")

then feed this to dsm() with the full segment data and the detection
function that has species as a covariate in it.

The DSM will then be fitted using only the babelfish observations.

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] strict vs weak monotonicity
messages.body_plain:
Antonela

In the absence of covariates in your detection function, the `ds()` function uses strict monotonicity as the default.  The term `strict` means checks are employed to make sure that the detection function is decreasing as a function of perpendicular distance.  That is the most plausible shape for the detection process; only under very unusual circumstances might the probability of detecting animals increase some distance away from the transect.

I suggest you keep with the default `strict` monotonicity constraint unless there is good reason to do otherwise.

Hi Mark, List,

You make some good points, but actually fear your clarification might have muddied the waters a bit, and so I'll comment on it.

It is very uncommon to have detectability not drop with distance. The only really obvious example I know of that is in the case of aerial surveys without a belly window, and then, a modal detection function might be more sensible. But dealing with that will take you away from conventional distance sampling. And if you are not in a situation where the usual assumptions hold (random transects with respect to animals, g0=1, no measurement error, observation can be approximated by a snapshot - but go to the books for a complete description), then I suspect that monotonicity constraints are the least of your worries: you need to first understand what might have gone wrong and what will be the impact, and if it is possible, or not, to salvage the data.

One should not confuse the probability of detection with the availability of animals to be detected. These two concepts, and their corresponding functions, are intertwined in conventional methods and cannot be separated out (without additional independent information), but they should not be confused. What you see in the data, e.g. a perhaps not decreasing function, will not be just detectability, in that case it is much more likely something to do with availability, most likely animal movement or transects placed not at random.

If animals move away from your line prior to detection, then strictly, conceptually, I prefer to see that as having little to do with the detection probability. It changes the availability of animals to be detected. But conditional on the position of where the animal happens to be, it's detectability should be a function of distance and decrease with distance.

The aspect of different habitats is also a separate issue. Sure you can have say two habitats, and in one detections are easier than in the other. Then you might have an animal as 100 meters from the line in "visible" habitat being easier to see than one at 20 meters from the line in "hard" habitat. But that does not mean detection is easier at 100 meters than 20. Once averaged out across all possible animals that will be at either 20 or 100 meters, unconditional of the habitat they are in, they should be easier to see at 20. So here what you want is to include a habitat covariate, not play with monotonicity constraints.

My final advice, and to come back to the question originally asked: if you have to ask, and that's just fine of course, then you almost for sure don't want to remove the monotonicity constraints. You only do that if you fully understand what might be going on with your data and what are the consequences of doing so. In 99% of the cases, you do NOT want to do it. And the number of statistics that are made up just increased a bit...

Cheers

T

messages.body_plain:
Antonela

Nothing wrong with your unit conversion factor.

I don't claim to have done a comprehensive analysis of the data you provided.  However, I suspect the key to differences you may have derived from Distance for Windows stems from the handling of group size.  Your group sizes range from 1 to 1200, leading me to suspect the existence of size bias in your analysis.  You provide a graph of group size as a function of distance, but only out to a distance of 300m; it is what happens beyond that, namely absence of small groups at large distances, that leads to an estimate of average group size that is too large (i.e., size bias).

I suspect when you performed your analysis in Distance for Windows you invoked the size bias regression procedure, that cancels this size bias in average group size.

To do a similar thing in R, you would use group size as a covariate in the detection function.  For the analyses I performed on your data, I looked only at the hazard rate model and used visual inspection of your perpendicular distance histogram to truncate just before 800m (at 770m).  Here are two models: with and without size as a covariate:

cu <- convert_units("meter", "kilometer", "square kilometer")
erictrun770 <- ds(oct08, key="hr", convert=cu, truncation = 770)
summary(erictrun770)
gof_ds(erictrun770)
plot(erictrun770)
ericsize770 <- ds(oct08, key="hr", convert=cu, truncation=770, formula=~size)
gof_ds(ericsize770)
summary(ericsize770)
plot(ericsize770)

There is some lack of fit of the ~size model (perhaps further truncation is in order), but the delta-AIC value for the model without ~size is 125; a compelling argument that detectability is influenced by group size.

Examining the estimates of expected group size under the two models, we see the result of size bias and likely the cause of the discrepancy between this analysis and Distance for Windows analysis.

messages.body_plain:
Antonela

The KS test is performed via bootstrap; i.e. repeated resampling the data (default number of replicates is 100).  If there is difficulty in fitting the detection function to a resampling of the data, the optimisation routine may fail to converge for that replicate.  It may be the case that gof_ds still computes a KS test statistic result, but without the offending replicate.  Can you check whether you have a KS result in the face of a replicate convergence failure?

Even if there is no KS test result, I believe there will be a Cramer-von Mises test result (that does not depend upon bootstrapping).  In my experience, the result of a KS goodness of fit test and the Cramer-von Mises goodness of fit test are essentially equivalent.  I can't think of an instance where one test has indicated good fit to data while the other indicated poor fit.  In other words, if you are having trouble with the KS test, information from the Cramer-von Mises test will be essentially equivalent.  I don't believe going down the route of rescaling will serve you in this instance.

Giles

There are several challenges associated with the comparison you desire.  First, the two density estimates are not independent--data from first five minutes are in both estimates.  That makes a clean comparison difficult.

Also recall that animal movement induces bias in density estimates (see Section 10.1.2 of Buckland et al. (2015)).  If animals move (which they do), waiting long enough animals will come past the observer.  The longer the sampling duration the higher the density estimate.  This is the case in your data for 24 of the 28 species.

Finally, note the precision in most density estimates produces are large relative to the differences observed.  I provide a bit of R code looking at your spreadsheet results.  It produces the magnitude of the density estimates relative to the standard error of the 10minute estimate.  As a rule of thumb, if these values exceed 1.96, you might suggest the difference is statistically meaningful.  Five species (COLPAL, CUCCAN, LUSMEG, TURMER, TURPHI) exceed that threshold.
